notes.h: Renal physiology: filtration, tubular handling and clearance
notes.body:
The kidneys receive about 20% of cardiac output. Each nephron filters plasma at the glomerulus and then modifies the filtrate along the tubule.

Filtration depends on Starling forces: net filtration pressure = glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure − Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure − glomerular oncotic pressure. The filtration barrier (fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocyte slit diaphragms) restricts molecules by size and negative charge, so albumin is normally largely retained. Normal GFR is about 120 mL/min (around 180 L/day).

Autoregulation keeps GFR stable across a wide range of blood pressures through the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback (the macula densa senses NaCl delivery and adjusts afferent arteriolar tone). Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, supporting GFR when perfusion falls; prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole. This is why ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs together can precipitate acute kidney injury in a dehydrated patient.

Tubular segments:
- Proximal tubule: reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered sodium and water, nearly all glucose (SGLT2, SGLT1), amino acids and most bicarbonate. Glucose appears in urine once the transport maximum is exceeded.
- Loop of Henle: the thick ascending limb reabsorbs NaCl via the Na-K-2Cl co-transporter (NKCC2) but is impermeable to water, generating the medullary gradient by countercurrent multiplication. Loop diuretics block NKCC2.
- Distal convoluted tubule: Na-Cl co-transporter (target of thiazides); PTH-regulated calcium reabsorption.
- Collecting duct: principal cells reabsorb sodium via ENaC under aldosterone and secrete potassium; ADH inserts aquaporin-2. Intercalated cells secrete H⁺ or bicarbonate.

Clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute: C = (U × V) ÷ P. Inulin clearance equals GFR because it is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted. Creatinine slightly overestimates GFR because a little is secreted. In practice eGFR is calculated from creatinine using the CKD-EPI equation (NICE NG203); cystatin C can help where muscle mass is unusual.

Worked example: urine creatinine 8 mmol/L, urine flow 1.5 mL/min, plasma creatinine 0.1 mmol/L (100 µmol/L). Clearance = (8 × 1.5) ÷ 0.1 = 120 mL/min.

The kidney is also an endocrine organ: renin (juxtaglomerular cells), erythropoietin (peritubular fibroblasts), and 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D.

CKD (KDIGO) is classified by cause, GFR category (G1–G5, with G3 split into G3a and G3b) and albuminuria category (A1–A3), using the urine albumin:creatinine ratio. AKI (KDIGO) is a creatinine rise of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours, a rise to 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours or more.

Pitfalls:
- Mixing units when calculating clearance (µmol/L versus mmol/L).
- Forgetting that creatinine is a late, insensitive marker: GFR can halve before creatinine leaves the reference range.
- Using eGFR in AKI, where creatinine is not at steady state.

Total body water is about 60% of body weight in adult men (less in women and older people): two-thirds intracellular and one-third extracellular, of which a quarter is plasma. Water moves freely between compartments to equalise osmolality; sodium is the main extracellular osmole and potassium the main intracellular one.

Plasma osmolality is about 275–295 mOsm/kg and can be estimated as 2Na + glucose + urea. The osmolar gap (measured minus calculated) rises with unmeasured osmoles such as ethanol, methanol and ethylene glycol.

Fluid prescribing (NICE CG174): assess need for resuscitation, routine maintenance or replacement. Routine maintenance in adults is roughly 25–30 mL/kg/day water with about 1 mmol/kg/day each of sodium, potassium and chloride, and 50–100 g/day glucose to limit ketosis. Resuscitation uses a balanced crystalloid or 0.9% sodium chloride in boluses with reassessment. Large volumes of 0.9% saline cause hyperchloraemic acidosis.

Hyponatraemia (sodium below 135 mmol/L) is a disorder of water balance. Approach:
- Confirm hypotonicity (exclude hyperglycaemia and pseudohyponatraemia).
- Check urine osmolality: below 100 mOsm/kg suggests primary polydipsia or low solute intake.
- Assess volume status and urine sodium: hypovolaemic with low urine sodium suggests extrarenal loss; high urine sodium suggests diuretics or adrenal insufficiency; hypervolaemic states include heart failure, cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome; euvolaemic suggests SIADH, hypothyroidism or glucocorticoid deficiency.
- Severe symptoms (seizures, reduced consciousness) need hypertonic saline boluses. Correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly, by no more than about 10 mmol/L in 24 hours (lower in high-risk patients), to avoid osmotic demyelination.

Hypernatraemia almost always reflects water deficit in people who cannot access water or have AVP deficiency or resistance; correct gradually.

Potassium: about 98% is intracellular, held there by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Insulin, beta-2 agonists and alkalosis shift K⁺ into cells; acidosis and cell lysis shift it out. Renal excretion depends on aldosterone and distal sodium delivery.
- Hyperkalaemia causes: AKI and CKD, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, MR antagonists, potassium-sparing diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, rhabdomyolysis, and haemolysed samples. ECG: tall tented T waves, flattened P waves, wide QRS, sine wave, then arrest.
- Emergency management (UK Kidney Association): IV calcium stabilises the myocardium; insulin with glucose shifts K⁺ into cells; salbutamol as an adjunct; then remove potassium with binders (e.g. sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or patiromer) or dialysis and treat the cause.
- Hypokalaemia causes: diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea, hyperaldosteronism, refeeding. ECG: flat T waves and U waves. Correct magnesium as well, since hypomagnesaemia causes renal potassium wasting.

Worked example: Na 120, glucose 5, urea 5 gives calculated osmolality 2 × 120 + 5 + 5 = 250 mOsm/kg, confirming hypotonic hyponatraemia.

Pitfalls: correcting sodium too quickly; forgetting that calcium does not lower potassium; treating a haemolysed sample; prescribing maintenance fluids without considering oral intake or ongoing losses.

notes.h: Acid-base balance and blood gas interpretation
notes.body:
Arterial pH is kept near 7.35–7.45. The bicarbonate buffer system links the lungs and kidneys: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] ÷ (0.03 × pCO₂)) with pCO₂ in mmHg (0.23 × pCO₂ in kPa).

The kidneys reabsorb filtered bicarbonate (mainly proximally, via carbonic anhydrase) and generate new bicarbonate by excreting H⁺ as titratable acid and ammonium. The lungs adjust CO₂ within minutes; renal compensation takes days.

Stepwise interpretation:
- Is the patient acidaemic or alkalaemic?
- Is the primary process respiratory (pCO₂ moves in the direction that explains the pH) or metabolic (bicarbonate does)?
- Is compensation appropriate? For metabolic acidosis, Winter's formula predicts pCO₂ (mmHg) = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2. A pCO₂ higher than predicted means a co-existing respiratory acidosis.
- In metabolic acidosis, calculate the anion gap: Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), normally about 8–16 mmol/L depending on the laboratory. Correct for low albumin (it falls by about 2.5 mmol/L per 10 g/L albumin fall).
- Check oxygenation separately.

High anion gap metabolic acidosis: lactate (shock, sepsis, metformin), ketoacidosis (diabetic, alcoholic, starvation), renal failure, and toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate). An increased osmolar gap points to a toxic alcohol.

Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis: diarrhoea, ileostomy losses, renal tubular acidosis, large-volume saline, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. The urine anion gap helps: negative in diarrhoea (ammonium excretion intact), positive in distal RTA.
- Type 1 (distal) RTA: failure of H⁺ secretion; hypokalaemia, urine pH above 5.5, stones and nephrocalcinosis.
- Type 2 (proximal): bicarbonate wasting, often with Fanconi syndrome.
- Type 4: hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance, with hyperkalaemia (often diabetic nephropathy).

Metabolic alkalosis: vomiting or nasogastric loss, diuretics, hyperaldosteronism. Volume depletion maintains it because the kidney reabsorbs sodium with bicarbonate; urine chloride is low in saline-responsive causes.

Respiratory acidosis: hypoventilation (COPD, opioids, neuromuscular weakness). Respiratory alkalosis: hyperventilation (anxiety, pulmonary embolism, early salicylate poisoning, pregnancy, high altitude).

Worked example: pH 7.24, pCO₂ 3.2 kPa (24 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 10, Na 140, Cl 104. Anion gap = 140 − 114 = 26 (raised). Predicted pCO₂ = 1.5 × 10 + 8 = 23 ± 2 mmHg, so respiratory compensation is appropriate. Diagnosis: high anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation; check lactate, ketones and renal function.

Pitfalls: calling compensation 'complete' (it rarely returns pH to normal); mixing kPa and mmHg in formulas; ignoring a low albumin that hides a raised anion gap; forgetting that salicylate causes both respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis.

notes.h: Upper GI tract: oesophagus, stomach and duodenum
notes.body:
Swallowing moves food through the upper oesophageal sphincter and by peristalsis to the lower oesophageal sphincter, which relaxes via inhibitory nitric oxide and VIP neurons.

Gastric acid is secreted by parietal cells using the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump). Three stimuli act on the parietal cell: acetylcholine (vagal, M3), gastrin (from antral G cells, acting partly via ECL cells) and histamine (from ECL cells, H2 receptors). Somatostatin from D cells inhibits. Parietal cells also secrete intrinsic factor, essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen. The cephalic, gastric and intestinal phases describe how secretion is triggered by anticipation, gastric distension and peptides, and duodenal feedback.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: heartburn and regurgitation due to transient sphincter relaxation, hiatus hernia or impaired clearance. Treat with lifestyle change and proton pump inhibitors (irreversible H⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition). Barrett's oesophagus is metaplasia of squamous to columnar epithelium with intestinal features, a precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and is kept under endoscopic surveillance.

Dysphagia: progressive dysphagia to solids then liquids with weight loss suggests malignancy; dysphagia to both from the start suggests a motility disorder. Achalasia is failure of LOS relaxation with loss of peristalsis due to loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons; diagnose with high-resolution manometry; barium shows a 'bird's beak'. Eosinophilic oesophagitis causes food bolus obstruction in young atopic men.

Peptic ulcer disease: mainly Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs (which reduce protective prostaglandins through COX-1 inhibition). Test for H. pylori with urea breath test or stool antigen, after stopping PPIs for 2 weeks. Eradication uses a PPI with two antibiotics for 7 days (NICE CG184). Retest after eradication where appropriate.

Upper GI bleeding: haematemesis or melaena. Risk stratify with the Glasgow-Blatchford score (low scores may be managed as outpatients); resuscitate; endoscopy within 24 hours of admission (immediately after resuscitation if unstable). Suspected variceal bleeding needs terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics before endoscopy, then band ligation.

Red flag referral (NICE NG12): urgent direct access endoscopy for dysphagia, or for people 55 and over with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia.

Gastric cancer is usually adenocarcinoma linked to H. pylori and atrophic gastritis. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma, associated with MEN1) causes multiple refractory ulcers and diarrhoea.

Applied illustration: a 72-year-old taking naproxen presents with melaena, Hb 84 g/L, pulse 110 and BP 96/60 mmHg. He is shocked, scores high on Glasgow-Blatchford and needs resuscitation, transfusion as indicated and urgent endoscopy; a bleeding duodenal ulcer is likely.

Pitfalls: testing for H. pylori on a PPI (false negatives); assuming dyspepsia in an older person is benign; giving PPIs before endoscopy in place of urgent endoscopy (NICE advises against routine pre-endoscopy PPIs in non-variceal bleeding).

notes.h: Lower GI tract: small bowel, colon and inflammatory disease
notes.body:
The small intestine is the main site of digestion and absorption. Villi and microvilli increase surface area; brush border enzymes complete carbohydrate and peptide digestion. Glucose and galactose enter via SGLT1 (the basis of oral rehydration solution), fructose via GLUT5. Fat requires bile salts for micelles and pancreatic lipase. Iron and folate are absorbed proximally; vitamin B12 and bile salts in the terminal ileum. The colon absorbs water and electrolytes and hosts microbial fermentation.

Diarrhoea is classified as osmotic (stops with fasting; lactose intolerance, laxatives), secretory (continues with fasting; cholera toxin raises cAMP and opens CFTR chloride channels), inflammatory (blood, fever) or due to dysmotility.

Coeliac disease: immune response to gluten in genetically susceptible people (HLA-DQ2 or DQ8), causing villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia. Test with IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody and total IgA while eating gluten; confirm with duodenal biopsy (BSG guidance allows a no-biopsy route in selected cases). Treat with a lifelong gluten-free diet. Associations include iron deficiency, osteoporosis, dermatitis herpetiformis and small bowel lymphoma.

Inflammatory bowel disease:
- Crohn's disease: any part of the gut, skip lesions, transmural inflammation, granulomas, fistulae and strictures; smoking worsens it. Terminal ileal disease causes B12 and bile salt malabsorption.
- Ulcerative colitis: continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum proximally, bloody diarrhoea; smoking appears protective; associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis.
- Faecal calprotectin helps distinguish IBD from IBS. Treatment classes: aminosalicylates (UC), corticosteroids for flares (not maintenance), thiopurines and methotrexate, biologics (anti-TNF, anti-integrin, anti-IL-12/23), and JAK inhibitors. Acute severe UC (Truelove and Witts criteria) needs admission, IV steroids and early surgical review.

Irritable bowel syndrome: recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation with altered stool form or frequency, without red flags. A positive diagnosis is made after basic tests (blood count, CRP, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin) (NICE CG61).

Colorectal cancer: most arise from adenomas through the adenoma-carcinoma sequence (APC, KRAS, TP53). Hereditary forms include familial adenomatous polyposis and Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair defects). NICE DG56 uses faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) to triage symptomatic patients; urgent referral if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g or more. The NHS bowel screening programme uses home FIT.

Other conditions: diverticular disease (sigmoid, low-fibre diets), acute mesenteric ischaemia (pain out of proportion to signs, raised lactate, often with AF), and large bowel obstruction from cancer or volvulus.

Applied illustration: a 24-year-old with 6 weeks of bloody diarrhoea, 8 stools a day, pulse 102, temperature 37.9°C and raised CRP meets criteria for acute severe ulcerative colitis and needs admission.

Pitfalls: testing for coeliac disease after gluten has been stopped; labelling IBS without excluding red flags; using steroids for maintenance in IBD.

The liver receives about 75% of its blood from the portal vein and the rest from the hepatic artery. Its functions include protein synthesis (albumin, clotting factors II, VII, IX, X), glucose homeostasis, drug metabolism (phase I cytochrome P450 oxidation, phase II conjugation), bile production and bilirubin conjugation.

Bilirubin is formed from haem, carried to the liver bound to albumin, conjugated by UDP-glucuronyltransferase and excreted in bile. Gut bacteria convert it to urobilinogen, some of which is reabsorbed and excreted in urine.
- Pre-hepatic (haemolysis, Gilbert's syndrome): raised unconjugated bilirubin, no bilirubinuria.
- Hepatocellular (hepatitis, drugs, alcohol): mixed, with high transaminases.
- Post-hepatic or cholestatic (gallstones, pancreatic cancer, PBC, PSC): conjugated bilirubin with dark urine, pale stools and itch; ALP and GGT dominate.

'Liver function tests' are mostly markers of injury: ALT and AST (hepatocellular), ALP and GGT (cholestasis). True synthetic function is shown by albumin and prothrombin time (INR).

Chronic liver disease: in the UK the main causes are alcohol-related liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly NAFLD) and viral hepatitis (B and C). Fibrosis risk in MASLD is stratified with the FIB-4 score followed by the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test or transient elastography. Other causes include haemochromatosis, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis (anti-mitochondrial antibodies, treated with ursodeoxycholic acid), primary sclerosing cholangitis, Wilson's disease and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

Cirrhosis complications:
- Portal hypertension: varices (non-selective beta-blocker or banding for primary prevention), splenomegaly.
- Ascites: from portal hypertension and renal sodium retention. A serum-ascites albumin gradient of 11 g/L or more indicates portal hypertension. Treat with sodium restriction and spironolactone; large-volume paracentesis with albumin replacement. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed by ascitic neutrophils above 250 cells/mm³.
- Hepatic encephalopathy: ammonia and other gut toxins; treat precipitants, lactulose, rifaximin.
- Hepatorenal syndrome, coagulopathy and hepatocellular carcinoma (six-monthly ultrasound surveillance).
- Prognosis: Child-Pugh and MELD scores.

Acute liver failure: jaundice, coagulopathy and encephalopathy without prior liver disease; in the UK paracetamol overdose is the leading cause. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI. King's College criteria guide transplant referral.

Biliary disease: gallstones (mostly cholesterol) cause biliary colic, acute cholecystitis (Murphy's sign, fever), choledocholithiasis and ascending cholangitis (Charcot's triad: fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain), and gallstone pancreatitis. Ultrasound is first line; MRCP images the ducts; ERCP is therapeutic. Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests malignant obstruction (Courvoisier's law).

Applied illustration: bilirubin 30 µmol/L, unconjugated, normal enzymes and blood count, rising when fasting or unwell: Gilbert's syndrome, which needs reassurance only.

Pitfalls: equating raised transaminases with poor liver function; forgetting that a normal LFT panel does not exclude cirrhosis; giving sedatives in hepatic encephalopathy.

notes.h: Nutrition: assessment, micronutrients and nutritional support
notes.body:
Malnutrition includes undernutrition and overnutrition. NICE CG32 defines undernutrition as BMI below 18.5 kg/m², unintentional weight loss over 10% in 3–6 months, or BMI below 20 with over 5% loss. Screen hospital and care home patients with the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), which combines BMI, recent weight loss and acute disease effect.

Energy balance: total energy expenditure = basal metabolic rate (about 60–70%) + thermic effect of food (about 10%) + physical activity. Energy yields: carbohydrate and protein about 4 kcal/g, fat 9 kcal/g, alcohol 7 kcal/g.

Macronutrient deficiency in children: marasmus (energy deficit, wasting) and kwashiorkor (oedema, fatty liver, skin changes, linked to protein deficiency and other factors).

Key micronutrients:
- Thiamine (B1): Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) and beriberi; high risk in alcohol misuse; give parenteral thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients.
- B12: macrocytic anaemia, subacute combined degeneration of the cord; causes include pernicious anaemia (intrinsic factor antibodies), ileal resection, metformin and veganism.
- Folate: macrocytic anaemia; neural tube defects; supplementation before conception.
- Vitamin C: scurvy with perifollicular haemorrhage and gum disease (collagen hydroxylation).
- Vitamin D: rickets and osteomalacia.
- Vitamin K: clotting factor deficiency, important in neonates and cholestasis.
- Vitamin A: night blindness. Iron: microcytic anaemia. Zinc: dermatitis and poor wound healing. Niacin (B3): pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia).

Nutritional support (NICE CG32): use the gut if it works. Options escalate from food fortification and oral supplements, to enteral tube feeding (nasogastric, then gastrostomy for longer-term needs), to parenteral nutrition when the gut cannot absorb enough (intestinal failure, obstruction, high-output fistula). Parenteral nutrition carries risks of line sepsis, thrombosis, metabolic derangement and liver dysfunction.

Refeeding syndrome: after starvation, feeding (especially carbohydrate) triggers insulin release, driving phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and increasing thiamine use. Severe hypophosphataemia can cause heart failure, arrhythmia, respiratory failure and seizures. High-risk patients (very low BMI, minimal intake for over 10 days, rapid weight loss, low baseline electrolytes, alcohol misuse) start feeding slowly with thiamine and B vitamins, electrolyte replacement and daily monitoring.

Worked example: a man who now weighs 70 kg has lost 9 kg over 3 months. Weight loss = 9 ÷ 79 = about 11.4% of his original weight, meeting the NICE weight-loss criterion for malnutrition.

Pitfalls:
- Calculating weight loss against current rather than original weight.
- Starting full feeding in high-risk patients.
- Giving folic acid alone in combined deficiency, which can worsen B12-related neuropathy.
- Forgetting that BMI may be falsely reassuring with oedema or ascites.

Fuel metabolism switches between fed and fasting states under the insulin-glucagon ratio.
- Fed state: insulin promotes glucose uptake, glycolysis, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis and protein synthesis.
- Early fasting: glucagon drives hepatic glycogenolysis; liver glycogen lasts roughly 24 hours.
- Prolonged fasting: gluconeogenesis from lactate (Cori cycle), glycerol and amino acids (alanine); lipolysis supplies fatty acids, which the liver converts to ketones. With time the brain adapts to use ketones, sparing muscle protein.

Key pathways: glycolysis produces pyruvate; aerobic metabolism via pyruvate dehydrogenase, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation yields most ATP; beta-oxidation breaks down fatty acids in mitochondria (carnitine shuttle). The pentose phosphate pathway makes NADPH; G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-induced haemolysis.

Inborn errors illustrate the pathways: phenylketonuria (phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, detected on newborn blood spot screening, treated by diet), glycogen storage diseases (von Gierke's: fasting hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis), MCAD deficiency (hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting or illness), and urea cycle defects (hyperammonaemia).

Lipids: chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride; VLDL carries hepatic triglyceride and becomes LDL, which delivers cholesterol via LDL receptors; HDL mediates reverse cholesterol transport. Familial hypercholesterolaemia (LDL receptor, APOB or PCSK9 mutations) causes very high LDL, tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease; cascade testing of relatives is recommended. Lipid-lowering classes: statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors), ezetimibe (blocks intestinal NPC1L1), PCSK9 inhibitors, and inclisiran (siRNA against PCSK9).

Obesity: BMI 30 kg/m² or more (lower thresholds, from 27.5, for people of South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean origin). Waist-to-height ratio of 0.5 or more indicates increased central adiposity. Appetite is regulated by the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus: leptin from adipose tissue and gut hormones (GLP-1, PYY) promote satiety; ghrelin stimulates hunger. Monogenic obesity (leptin, leptin receptor or MC4R defects) is rare.

Complications include type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, MASLD, obstructive sleep apnoea, osteoarthritis, some cancers and PCOS.

Management (NICE NG246, Overweight and obesity management, 2025, which replaced CG189 and related guidance): multicomponent lifestyle interventions; drug classes including GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide), the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide, and orlistat (pancreatic lipase inhibitor), each within the criteria of its NICE technology appraisal; and bariatric surgery (sleeve gastrectomy, Roux-en-Y bypass) for selected people, generally BMI 40 or more, or 35–40 with significant comorbidity, with expedited assessment for recent-onset type 2 diabetes.

Metabolic syndrome describes clustering of central obesity, raised triglycerides, low HDL, hypertension and impaired glucose.

Worked example: 102 kg and 1.75 m gives BMI = 102 ÷ 1.75² = 102 ÷ 3.0625 ≈ 33.3 kg/m² (obesity class I).

Pitfalls: treating BMI as a measure of adiposity in muscular people; forgetting ethnicity-adjusted thresholds; ignoring nutritional deficiencies after bariatric surgery.

cards.f: State the clearance formula.
cards.b: C = (U × V) ÷ P, where U is urine concentration, V urine flow rate and P plasma concentration; units of mL/min.

cards.f: Why does inulin clearance equal GFR?
cards.b: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so all of it in urine came from filtration.

cards.f: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate GFR?
cards.b: A small amount of creatinine is secreted by the proximal tubule, adding to the filtered load.

cards.f: How does angiotensin II maintain GFR when renal perfusion falls?
cards.b: It preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole, raising glomerular capillary pressure.

cards.f: What is tubuloglomerular feedback?
cards.b: The macula densa senses NaCl delivery to the distal tubule; high delivery causes afferent arteriolar constriction, lowering GFR.

cards.f: Which transporter do loop diuretics block and where?
cards.b: The Na-K-2Cl co-transporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

cards.f: Where do thiazide diuretics act?
cards.b: The Na-Cl co-transporter in the distal convoluted tubule.

cards.f: KDIGO definition of acute kidney injury?
cards.b: Creatinine rise of at least 26 µmol/L within 48 hours, or to 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours or more.

cards.f: How is CKD classified?
cards.b: By cause, GFR category (G1–G5) and albuminuria category (A1–A3) using the urine albumin:creatinine ratio.

cards.f: Why is the thick ascending limb essential to urine concentration?
cards.b: It pumps NaCl out without water, generating the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium by countercurrent multiplication, which lets ADH-driven water reabsorption concentrate urine.

cards.f: Approximate distribution of total body water in an adult?
cards.b: About 60% of body weight in men; two-thirds intracellular, one-third extracellular, with plasma about a quarter of extracellular fluid.

cards.f: Formula for calculated plasma osmolality?
cards.b: 2 × Na + glucose + urea (all in mmol/L).

cards.f: What does a raised osmolar gap suggest?
cards.b: Unmeasured osmoles such as ethanol, methanol, ethylene glycol or mannitol.

cards.f: Adult routine maintenance fluid requirement (NICE CG174)?
cards.b: About 25–30 mL/kg/day of water, around 1 mmol/kg/day each of sodium, potassium and chloride, and 50–100 g/day glucose.

cards.f: Main risk of correcting chronic hyponatraemia too quickly?
cards.b: Osmotic demyelination syndrome, so the rise is limited to about 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, less in high-risk patients.

cards.f: Urine osmolality below 100 mOsm/kg in hyponatraemia suggests what?
cards.b: Appropriately suppressed ADH: primary polydipsia, beer potomania or low solute intake.

cards.f: First drug given for hyperkalaemia with ECG changes and its purpose?
cards.b: IV calcium (gluconate or chloride) to stabilise the myocardium; it does not lower serum potassium.

cards.f: How does insulin lower serum potassium?
cards.b: It stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, shifting potassium into cells; glucose is given with it to prevent hypoglycaemia.

cards.f: ECG changes of hypokalaemia?
cards.b: Flattened T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves and a prolonged apparent QT; risk of arrhythmia.

cards.f: Why replace magnesium in refractory hypokalaemia?
cards.b: Low magnesium increases renal potassium secretion via ROMK channels, so potassium will not correct until magnesium is replaced.

cards.f: Formula for the anion gap?
cards.b: Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); a typical reference range is about 8–16 mmol/L, depending on the laboratory.

cards.f: What does Winter's formula predict?
cards.b: Expected pCO₂ in metabolic acidosis: pCO₂ (mmHg) = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2. A higher pCO₂ indicates co-existing respiratory acidosis.

cards.f: Name four causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
cards.b: Lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, renal failure and toxins such as methanol, ethylene glycol or salicylate.

cards.f: Name three causes of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
cards.b: Diarrhoea or ileostomy loss, renal tubular acidosis and large-volume 0.9% saline infusion.

cards.f: Features of type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis?
cards.b: Impaired distal H⁺ secretion: hypokalaemia, urine pH persistently above 5.5, renal stones and nephrocalcinosis.

cards.f: What is type 4 renal tubular acidosis?
cards.b: Hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance causing hyperkalaemic normal anion gap acidosis, often in diabetic nephropathy or with ACE inhibitors.

cards.f: Why does vomiting cause metabolic alkalosis?
cards.b: Loss of gastric HCl leaves bicarbonate behind; volume depletion and hypokalaemia make the kidney retain bicarbonate, maintaining the alkalosis.

cards.f: What acid-base pattern does salicylate poisoning cause?
cards.b: An early respiratory alkalosis from direct respiratory stimulation, followed by a high anion gap metabolic acidosis; often both together.

cards.f: How do the lungs and kidneys differ in speed of compensation?
cards.b: Respiratory compensation occurs within minutes to hours; renal compensation takes several days.

cards.f: Why correct the anion gap for albumin?
cards.b: Albumin is the main unmeasured anion; hypoalbuminaemia lowers the gap (about 2.5 mmol/L per 10 g/L fall) and can hide a high anion gap acidosis.

cards.f: Three main stimulants of parietal cell acid secretion?
cards.b: Acetylcholine (vagal, M3 receptors), gastrin and histamine (H2 receptors from ECL cells).

cards.f: Mechanism of proton pump inhibitors?
cards.b: They irreversibly inhibit the parietal cell H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, the final step of acid secretion.

cards.f: What is Barrett's oesophagus?
cards.b: Replacement of the normal squamous lining of the lower oesophagus with columnar epithelium with intestinal metaplasia, predisposing to adenocarcinoma.

cards.f: Pathophysiology of achalasia?
cards.b: Loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons causes failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis.

cards.f: Two commonest causes of peptic ulcer disease?
cards.b: Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID use.

cards.f: Why must PPIs be stopped before H. pylori testing?
cards.b: PPIs suppress the organism and can cause false negative urea breath and stool antigen tests; stop for 2 weeks beforehand.

cards.f: Which score risk-stratifies upper GI bleeding at first presentation?
cards.b: The Glasgow-Blatchford score; the full Rockall score is used after endoscopy.

cards.f: What two treatments are given before endoscopy in suspected variceal bleeding?
cards.b: Terlipressin (vasoconstrictor) and prophylactic antibiotics.

cards.f: What is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?
cards.b: A gastrin-secreting tumour (gastrinoma) causing acid hypersecretion, multiple or refractory ulcers and diarrhoea; associated with MEN1.

cards.f: Where is vitamin B12 absorbed and what does it need?
cards.b: In the terminal ileum, bound to intrinsic factor secreted by gastric parietal cells.

cards.f: Which transporter underlies oral rehydration solution?
cards.b: SGLT1, which co-transports sodium with glucose, drawing water with it even in secretory diarrhoea.

cards.f: How do osmotic and secretory diarrhoea differ when fasting?
cards.b: Osmotic diarrhoea stops with fasting; secretory diarrhoea continues.

cards.f: How does cholera toxin cause diarrhoea?
cards.b: It permanently activates Gs, raising cAMP in enterocytes, which opens CFTR chloride channels and drives secretion of salt and water.

cards.f: First-line test for coeliac disease?
cards.b: IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA, while the patient is eating gluten.

cards.f: Histological features of coeliac disease?
cards.b: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.

cards.f: Distinguish Crohn's disease from ulcerative colitis histologically and anatomically.
cards.b: Crohn's: any part of the gut, skip lesions, transmural inflammation, granulomas. UC: continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum, crypt abscesses, no granulomas.

cards.f: Effect of smoking on Crohn's disease versus ulcerative colitis?
cards.b: Smoking worsens Crohn's disease but appears protective in ulcerative colitis.

cards.f: Role of faecal calprotectin?
cards.b: A marker of intestinal inflammation that helps distinguish IBD from irritable bowel syndrome in primary care.

cards.f: Truelove and Witts criteria for acute severe UC?
cards.b: Six or more bloody stools a day plus a systemic feature: pulse over 90, temperature over 37.8°C, Hb under 105 g/L or ESR over 30.

cards.f: What FIT result triggers urgent colorectal referral (NICE DG56)?
cards.b: Faecal haemoglobin of 10 µg Hb/g faeces or more in a symptomatic patient.

cards.f: Pattern of liver tests in cholestasis?
cards.b: Predominantly raised ALP and GGT, with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia if jaundiced.

cards.f: Which blood tests reflect true hepatic synthetic function?
cards.b: Albumin and prothrombin time (INR); transaminases reflect injury, not function.

cards.f: What is Gilbert's syndrome?
cards.b: Reduced UDP-glucuronyltransferase activity causing mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, worse with fasting or illness; benign.

cards.f: Why are urine dark and stools pale in obstructive jaundice?
cards.b: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and spills into urine, while no bilirubin reaches the gut to form stercobilin.

cards.f: Significance of a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 11 g/L or more?
cards.b: It indicates portal hypertension (e.g. cirrhosis, heart failure) rather than peritoneal causes such as malignancy or infection.

cards.f: Diagnostic threshold for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
cards.b: Ascitic fluid neutrophil count above 250 cells/mm³.

cards.f: How does N-acetylcysteine work in paracetamol overdose?
cards.b: It replenishes glutathione, which conjugates the toxic metabolite NAPQI.

cards.f: What is Charcot's triad?
cards.b: Fever (often with rigors), jaundice and right upper quadrant pain, indicating ascending cholangitis.

cards.f: Which antibody is characteristic of primary biliary cholangitis?
cards.b: Anti-mitochondrial antibody; first-line treatment is ursodeoxycholic acid.

cards.f: Treatments for hepatic encephalopathy?
cards.b: Treat precipitants (infection, bleeding, constipation, drugs), lactulose to reduce ammonia absorption, and rifaximin to prevent recurrence.

cards.f: NICE CG32 criteria for malnutrition?
cards.b: BMI below 18.5, unintentional weight loss over 10% in 3–6 months, or BMI below 20 with over 5% weight loss in 3–6 months.

cards.f: What does MUST assess?
cards.b: BMI, unintentional weight loss over 3–6 months and the effect of acute illness on intake, to give a malnutrition risk score.

cards.f: Energy yield of fat, carbohydrate, protein and alcohol per gram?
cards.b: Fat about 9 kcal, carbohydrate and protein about 4 kcal, alcohol about 7 kcal.

cards.f: Classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
cards.b: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia (or nystagmus) and ataxia, due to thiamine deficiency.

cards.f: Why give thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients?
cards.b: Glucose metabolism consumes thiamine as a cofactor and can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.

cards.f: Key electrolyte abnormality in refeeding syndrome and its cause?
cards.b: Hypophosphataemia, as insulin released on feeding drives phosphate into cells for glycolysis and ATP synthesis.

cards.f: Deficiency causing pellagra and its features?
cards.b: Niacin (vitamin B3): dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.

cards.f: Why is folic acid alone dangerous in combined B12 and folate deficiency?
cards.b: It may correct the anaemia while B12-related neurological damage, such as subacute combined degeneration, progresses.

cards.f: When is parenteral rather than enteral nutrition indicated?
cards.b: When the gut is inaccessible or cannot absorb enough, e.g. intestinal failure, obstruction, prolonged ileus or high-output fistula.

cards.f: Why can BMI underestimate malnutrition?
cards.b: Oedema or ascites adds weight, and BMI does not distinguish fat from lean mass, so muscle loss can be hidden.

cards.f: How long do liver glycogen stores last during fasting?
cards.b: Roughly 24 hours, after which gluconeogenesis becomes the main source of glucose.

cards.f: What is the Cori cycle?
cards.b: Lactate from anaerobic glycolysis in muscle and red cells is converted back to glucose in the liver.

cards.f: Why does the brain use ketones in prolonged starvation?
cards.b: Adaptation to ketone bodies reduces the need for gluconeogenesis from amino acids, sparing muscle protein.

cards.f: Enzyme deficient in phenylketonuria and how it is detected?
cards.b: Phenylalanine hydroxylase; detected by newborn blood spot screening and treated with a low-phenylalanine diet.

cards.f: Why does MCAD deficiency cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia?
cards.b: Impaired beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids prevents ketone production and starves gluconeogenesis of energy during fasting.

cards.f: Genetic causes of familial hypercholesterolaemia?
cards.b: Mutations in the LDL receptor gene (most common), APOB or gain-of-function PCSK9.

cards.f: Mechanism of ezetimibe?
cards.b: It inhibits the NPC1L1 transporter, reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption.

cards.f: BMI threshold for obesity in people of South Asian origin (NICE)?
cards.b: 27.5 kg/m², lower than the general threshold of 30, because cardiometabolic risk occurs at lower BMI.

cards.f: Effects of leptin and ghrelin on appetite?
cards.b: Leptin from adipose tissue signals energy stores and suppresses appetite; ghrelin from the stomach stimulates hunger.

cards.f: Mechanism of orlistat?
cards.b: It inhibits pancreatic and gastric lipase, reducing fat absorption; side effects include steatorrhoea.

questions.q: Which nephron segment reabsorbs the largest fraction of filtered sodium?
questions.why: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered sodium and water; later segments fine-tune the remainder.

questions.q: A patient's potassium is 6.8 mmol/L with broad QRS complexes on the ECG. Which treatment acts fastest to protect the heart?
questions.why: IV calcium stabilises the cardiac membrane within minutes without lowering potassium; insulin-glucose then shifts potassium into cells, and binders remove it more slowly.

questions.q: A 75-year-old on a thiazide has sodium 121 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 252 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 410 mOsm/kg and urine sodium 48 mmol/L. She is clinically dry. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: SIADH is confirmed and fluid restriction is indicated
Thiazide-induced hyponatraemia; urine sodium is unreliable on diuretics
questions.why: SIADH cannot be diagnosed in a hypovolaemic patient on a diuretic, which itself raises urine sodium. Stopping the thiazide and cautious volume replacement are appropriate.

questions.q: Which condition causes a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis?
questions.why: Diarrhoea loses bicarbonate, which is replaced by chloride, giving a hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap acidosis. The others add unmeasured anions.

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.30, pCO₂ 3.6 kPa (27 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 13 mmol/L. Using Winter's formula, which statement is correct?
options: There is metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
There is a co-existing respiratory acidosis
There is a co-existing respiratory alkalosis
The primary disorder is respiratory alkalosis
questions.why: Predicted pCO₂ = 1.5 × 13 + 8 = 27.5 ± 2 mmHg. The measured 27 mmHg lies within this range, so compensation is appropriate.

questions.q: Which cell secretes intrinsic factor?
questions.why: Parietal cells secrete both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, so autoimmune destruction in pernicious anaemia causes B12 deficiency.

questions.q: Which feature is more typical of Crohn's disease than ulcerative colitis?
options: Continuous inflammation starting at the rectum
questions.why: Crohn's disease is transmural with skip lesions and granulomas; UC is continuous, mucosal and more strongly associated with PSC.

questions.q: A 45-year-old has bilirubin 98 µmol/L, ALT 64 U/L, ALP 720 U/L, GGT 610 U/L, dark urine and pale stools. Which investigation should come first?
questions.why: A cholestatic pattern needs ultrasound first to look for bile duct dilatation; dilated ducts suggest extrahepatic obstruction needing MRCP or ERCP, while undilated ducts prompt tests for intrahepatic causes.

questions.q: A man with alcohol dependence is admitted confused, with nystagmus and an unsteady gait. Which should be given first?
questions.why: This is likely Wernicke's encephalopathy. Parenteral thiamine is given promptly, before or with glucose, because glucose metabolism consumes thiamine.

questions.q: Which hormone stimulates appetite?
questions.why: Ghrelin is released by the stomach during fasting and stimulates hunger; the others promote satiety.

questions.q: A 3-year-old becomes drowsy after a day of vomiting and not eating. Glucose is 1.8 mmol/L and capillary ketones are undetectable. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.why: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting suggests a fatty acid oxidation defect such as MCAD deficiency. Normal fasting hypoglycaemia in a child is accompanied by high ketones.

questions.q: List three endocrine functions of the kidney.
markScheme: Renin secretion by juxtaglomerular cells (renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system)
Erythropoietin production by peritubular interstitial cells
1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol
questions.modelAnswer: The kidney releases renin from juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole in response to low perfusion, sympathetic stimulation and reduced distal sodium delivery, driving angiotensin II and aldosterone production. Peritubular fibroblast-like cells produce erythropoietin when oxygen delivery falls, which is why CKD causes anaemia. Proximal tubular cells convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active calcitriol under PTH stimulation, so CKD contributes to hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.q: A 24-hour urine collection is 1.8 L with creatinine 6 mmol/L. Plasma creatinine is 150 µmol/L. Calculate the creatinine clearance and comment on its relationship to GFR.
markScheme: Urine flow V = 1800 mL ÷ 1440 min = 1.25 mL/min
Plasma creatinine 150 µmol/L = 0.150 mmol/L (same units as urine)
Clearance = (6 × 1.25) ÷ 0.150 = 50 mL/min
Creatinine clearance overestimates GFR because of tubular secretion, especially as GFR falls; collection errors are common
questions.modelAnswer: Converting volume to flow gives 1800 ÷ 1440 = 1.25 mL/min. Using matching units, plasma creatinine is 0.150 mmol/L. Clearance = (U × V) ÷ P = (6 × 1.25) ÷ 0.150 = 50 mL/min. This approximates GFR but overestimates it, since some creatinine is secreted by the proximal tubule and this fraction rises as kidney function declines. Incomplete collection is a frequent source of error, which is why eGFR from creatinine, and sometimes cystatin C, is usually preferred.

questions.q: Describe the compartments of body water in a 70 kg man and explain where 1 L of IV 5% glucose distributes.
markScheme: Total body water about 60% of weight, roughly 42 L
Intracellular about two-thirds (about 28 L), extracellular about one-third (about 14 L)
Extracellular divides into interstitial (about three-quarters) and plasma (about one-quarter, about 3.5 L)
Glucose is metabolised leaving free water, which distributes through all compartments, so only about 1/12 (under 100 mL) stays in plasma
questions.modelAnswer: In a 70 kg man total body water is about 42 L: about 28 L intracellular and 14 L extracellular, the latter split into about 10.5 L interstitial fluid and 3.5 L plasma. Once infused, glucose is taken up and metabolised, leaving free water that distributes in proportion to total body water. Plasma is 3.5 of 42 L, roughly one-twelfth, so less than 100 mL of each litre remains intravascular. This is why 5% glucose is useless for resuscitation and, in excess, causes hyponatraemia.

questions.q: A 68-year-old with COPD is admitted drowsy with pneumonia and hypotension. Gas: pH 7.10, pCO₂ 7.2 kPa (54 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 16 mmol/L, Na 138, Cl 100, lactate 6 mmol/L. Interpret the result.
markScheme: Acidaemia (pH 7.10)
Low bicarbonate indicates metabolic acidosis; anion gap = 138 − (100 + 16) = 22 mmol/L, raised (lactic acidosis)
Winter's predicted pCO₂ = 1.5 × 16 + 8 = 32 ± 2 mmHg
Measured pCO₂ 54 mmHg is far higher, so there is a co-existing respiratory acidosis (ventilatory failure)
Mixed respiratory and high anion gap metabolic acidosis from sepsis with type 2 respiratory failure; needs urgent senior review and ventilatory support
questions.modelAnswer: The pH of 7.10 shows a severe acidaemia. Bicarbonate is low and the anion gap is 138 − 116 = 22 mmol/L, a high anion gap metabolic acidosis explained by lactate from septic shock. If the lungs were compensating, Winter's formula predicts pCO₂ of 1.5 × 16 + 8 = 32 ± 2 mmHg. Instead it is 54 mmHg, so there is also a primary respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation in COPD and drowsiness. This mixed acidosis is dangerous because neither system is compensating; he needs sepsis treatment, controlled oxygen and early consideration of ventilatory support.

questions.q: Give two drug classes that reduce gastric acid secretion and their molecular targets.
markScheme: Proton pump inhibitors: H⁺/K⁺-ATPase in parietal cells
H2-receptor antagonists: histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells
questions.modelAnswer: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, the final common pathway of acid secretion, and are the most potent acid suppressants. H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine competitively block histamine from ECL cells at parietal cell H2 receptors and reduce acid less completely.

questions.q: List three red-flag features in a patient with dyspepsia that warrant urgent referral under NICE NG12, and explain why age matters.
markScheme: Dysphagia (at any age)
Age 55 or over with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia
Upper abdominal mass consistent with stomach cancer (suspected cancer pathway referral)
Age matters because oesophageal and gastric cancer incidence rises steeply with age, so younger patients without alarm features are managed with test-and-treat or PPI first
questions.modelAnswer: NICE NG12 recommends urgent direct-access upper GI endoscopy for anyone with dysphagia and for people aged 55 or over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia. An upper abdominal mass suggesting stomach cancer warrants an urgent referral, and haematemesis needs same-day assessment. Age is part of the criteria because upper GI cancers are uncommon below 55, so younger people with uncomplicated dyspepsia are offered H. pylori testing or a trial of PPI rather than endoscopy.

questions.q: Explain why a patient who has had 60 cm of terminal ileum resected for Crohn's disease may develop diarrhoea, macrocytic anaemia and gallstones.
markScheme: The terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B12-intrinsic factor complexes; resection causes B12 deficiency and macrocytic anaemia
The terminal ileum reabsorbs bile salts; loss interrupts the enterohepatic circulation
Unabsorbed bile salts reach the colon and stimulate secretion, causing bile acid diarrhoea (treated with bile acid sequestrants)
Depleted bile salt pool makes bile supersaturated with cholesterol, predisposing to gallstones (and fat malabsorption if severe)
questions.modelAnswer: The terminal ileum is the only site of B12-intrinsic factor absorption, so resection leads to B12 deficiency, macrocytosis and potential neurological damage; lifelong parenteral B12 is usually needed. It also actively reabsorbs bile salts. When it is lost, bile salts spill into the colon, where they stimulate water and electrolyte secretion, causing bile acid diarrhoea that responds to sequestrants. The shrinking bile salt pool makes bile relatively supersaturated with cholesterol, increasing gallstone formation, and severe loss can cause steatorrhoea.

questions.q: Classify jaundice into three types, giving one cause of each.
markScheme: Pre-hepatic: haemolysis or Gilbert's syndrome (unconjugated)
Hepatic (hepatocellular): viral hepatitis, alcohol or drug-induced liver injury
Post-hepatic (obstructive): gallstones in the common bile duct or pancreatic head cancer
questions.modelAnswer: Pre-hepatic jaundice occurs when bilirubin production exceeds conjugating capacity or conjugation is impaired, as in haemolysis or Gilbert's syndrome, giving unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without bilirubin in the urine. Hepatic jaundice results from hepatocyte injury, for example viral hepatitis or paracetamol toxicity. Post-hepatic jaundice results from bile flow obstruction, such as choledocholithiasis or carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, causing conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, dark urine and pale stools.

questions.q: Explain the mechanism of liver injury in paracetamol overdose and how N-acetylcysteine prevents it. Why are some patients at higher risk?
markScheme: Normally paracetamol is mainly conjugated by glucuronidation and sulfation
A small fraction is oxidised by CYP2E1 (and CYP3A4) to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, normally detoxified by glutathione
In overdose conjugation saturates, more NAPQI forms and glutathione is depleted, so NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins causing centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis
N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione (and supports other protective pathways); most effective within 8 hours
Higher risk with depleted glutathione (malnutrition, eating disorders, chronic alcohol use) or enzyme induction; staggered overdoses are treated regardless of level
questions.modelAnswer: At therapeutic doses paracetamol is mostly glucuronidated and sulfated, while a small amount is oxidised by cytochrome P450 enzymes, mainly CYP2E1, to NAPQI, which glutathione neutralises. In overdose the conjugation pathways saturate, NAPQI production rises and glutathione becomes exhausted. NAPQI then binds cellular proteins, causing mitochondrial injury and necrosis concentrated in zone 3 around the central veins, where CYP2E1 is most abundant. N-acetylcysteine provides cysteine to regenerate glutathione and is nearly fully protective if given early, ideally within 8 hours. People with low glutathione reserves, such as the malnourished, and those with staggered ingestion are at greater risk.

questions.q: A woman 1.60 m tall weighs 46 kg; three months ago she weighed 54 kg. She is eating normally now. Calculate her BMI and percentage weight loss, give her MUST score and state its implication.
markScheme: Weight loss = 8 ÷ 54 ≈ 14.8% of original weight
MUST: BMI below 18.5 scores 2; weight loss over 10% scores 2; no acute disease effect scores 0; total 4
A score of 2 or more is high risk: refer to dietitian, treat, set goals and monitor
She meets NICE malnutrition criteria and two refeeding risk criteria (BMI under 18.5, weight loss over 10%), so feeding should be introduced cautiously
questions.modelAnswer: BMI is 46 ÷ 2.56, about 18.0 kg/m². She has lost 8 kg from an original 54 kg, which is 14.8%; percentage loss must be calculated against her original weight. On MUST, BMI below 18.5 scores 2 and weight loss over 10% scores 2, with no acute disease score, giving 4, which is high risk. She meets NICE criteria for malnutrition and needs dietetic referral, a nutrition care plan and monitoring. With BMI below 18.5 and weight loss above 10%, she also has two NICE risk factors for refeeding syndrome, so feeding should start cautiously with electrolyte monitoring and thiamine.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man has total cholesterol 9.8 mmol/L, HDL 1.2 mmol/L and triglycerides 1.8 mmol/L (fasting). He has Achilles tendon thickening and his father had a myocardial infarction at 44. Calculate his LDL, give the likely diagnosis and outline management.
markScheme: Friedewald: LDL = TC − HDL − (TG ÷ 2.2) = 9.8 − 1.2 − 0.82 ≈ 7.8 mmol/L (valid as TG below 4.5)
Tendon xanthomata with LDL above 4.9 mmol/L meet Simon Broome criteria for definite familial hypercholesterolaemia
Usually autosomal dominant mutation of LDL receptor (or APOB, PCSK9) reducing LDL clearance
Refer to specialist lipid clinic; DNA testing and cascade testing of first-degree relatives
High-intensity statin aiming for at least 50% LDL reduction, with ezetimibe, PCSK9-targeted therapy if needed; lifestyle and smoking advice
questions.modelAnswer: Using Friedewald, which is valid because triglycerides are below 4.5 mmol/L, LDL = 9.8 − 1.2 − (1.8 ÷ 2.2) = 9.8 − 1.2 − 0.82, about 7.8 mmol/L. An adult LDL above 4.9 mmol/L with tendon xanthomata meets Simon Broome criteria for definite familial hypercholesterolaemia, usually caused by an LDL receptor mutation inherited dominantly. He should be referred to a lipid clinic for genetic testing, and first-degree relatives offered cascade testing. Treatment starts with a high-intensity statin aiming for at least a 50% LDL fall, adding ezetimibe and, if needed, PCSK9-targeted therapy, together with lifestyle advice.

questions.q: Mrs Dawson, 78, has had three days of diarrhoea and poor intake. She takes ramipril and furosemide for heart failure and has been buying ibuprofen for knee pain. BP 92/54 mmHg, HR 104. Creatinine 300 µmol/L (baseline 110), K 6.2 mmol/L, urea 24 mmol/L. Urine Na 10 mmol/L, urine creatinine 12 mmol/L, plasma Na 138 mmol/L. (a) Stage the AKI. (b) Calculate the fractional excretion of sodium and interpret it. (c) Explain the pathophysiology. (d) Outline management.
markScheme: Creatinine ratio 300 ÷ 110 ≈ 2.7 times baseline: KDIGO stage 2 (2.0–2.9 times)
FENa = (urine Na × plasma Cr) ÷ (plasma Na × urine Cr) × 100, with creatinine in matching units
Below 1% suggests pre-renal AKI, though diuretics make FENa unreliable (urea excretion may be preferred)
Hypovolaemia reduces renal perfusion; NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation; ACE inhibitor removes angiotensin II efferent constriction, so GFR falls
Triple risk combination: diuretic, ACE inhibitor, NSAID
Treat hyperkalaemia: ECG, IV calcium if ECG changes, insulin-glucose, review potassium-raising drugs
Stop or withhold ACE inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID (sick-day guidance)
Careful IV fluid resuscitation with reassessment given heart failure; fluid balance and urine output monitoring
Urinalysis, renal ultrasound if obstruction suspected or no improvement; monitor creatinine and potassium; refer to renal team if no improvement or indications for dialysis
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Creatinine is 300 ÷ 110, about 2.7 times baseline, which is KDIGO stage 2 acute kidney injury.

(b) FENa = (urine Na × plasma creatinine) ÷ (plasma Na × urine creatinine) × 100. Converting plasma creatinine to 0.300 mmol/L: (10 × 0.300) ÷ (138 × 12) × 100 = 3 ÷ 1656 × 100, about 0.18%. A value below 1% suggests a pre-renal state with avid sodium retention. However, loop diuretics increase sodium excretion, so FENa must be interpreted cautiously; here it is low despite furosemide, supporting marked hypoperfusion.

(c) Diarrhoea and poor intake cause hypovolaemia and low renal perfusion. Normally GFR is protected by prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction. Ibuprofen removes the first and ramipril the second, while furosemide worsens volume depletion. This combination is a classic cause of AKI in older people. Reduced distal sodium delivery, ACE inhibition and reduced GFR all impair potassium excretion, explaining her hyperkalaemia.

(d) She needs an ECG; if there are hyperkalaemic changes, IV calcium is given, and insulin with glucose shifts potassium into cells. Ramipril, furosemide and ibuprofen are withheld. Fluid resuscitation with a crystalloid is given in small boluses with frequent review, because her heart failure creates a risk of pulmonary oedema. Fluid balance, urine output, daily weights and repeat creatinine and potassium are monitored. Urinalysis looks for blood and protein suggesting intrinsic disease, and a renal ultrasound is indicated if obstruction is possible or she fails to improve. Refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemic complications would prompt renal referral for dialysis. On recovery, medicines are restarted carefully and she is advised to avoid NSAIDs and follow sick-day rules.

questions.q: Mr Byrne, 71, is admitted after a seizure. He was diagnosed with small cell lung cancer last month. He is clinically euvolaemic. Na 118 mmol/L (two weeks ago 131), glucose 6 mmol/L, urea 3 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 248 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg, urine Na 62 mmol/L. TSH and cortisol are normal; he takes no diuretics. (a) Confirm the calculated osmolality and diagnosis. (b) Explain the pathophysiology. (c) Outline management, including safe correction.
markScheme: Calculated osmolality = 2 × 118 + 6 + 3 = 245 mOsm/kg, consistent with measured 248 (no osmolar gap): hypotonic hyponatraemia
Euvolaemia, inappropriately concentrated urine, urine Na above 30, normal thyroid/adrenal and no diuretics: SIADH
Likely ectopic ADH secretion from small cell lung cancer
ADH acts on V2 receptors, inserting aquaporin-2; water retention dilutes sodium; natriuresis via volume-mediated mechanisms keeps the patient clinically euvolaemic
Seizure indicates severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (cerebral oedema); the fall has developed over more than 48 hours, so it is chronic and at risk of osmotic demyelination if over-corrected
Immediate hypertonic saline boluses per protocol aiming for a rise of about 5 mmol/L to relieve symptoms, in a monitored setting
Limit correction to no more than about 10 mmol/L in 24 hours (8 in high-risk) to avoid osmotic demyelination
Frequent sodium checks (e.g. every few hours initially); if overcorrection occurs, give water or desmopressin to re-lower
Longer term: fluid restriction; treat the tumour (chemotherapy); consider V2 receptor antagonist (tolvaptan) or oral urea under specialist guidance
Avoid hypotonic fluids and review causative drugs
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Calculated osmolality = 2 × 118 + 6 + 3 = 245 mOsm/kg, matching the measured 248 mOsm/kg, so this is true hypotonic hyponatraemia with no osmolar gap. He is euvolaemic, his urine is inappropriately concentrated, urine sodium exceeds 30 mmol/L, thyroid and adrenal function are normal and he takes no diuretics. This meets the criteria for SIADH, most likely from ectopic ADH secretion by small cell lung cancer.

(b) ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells, increasing cAMP and inserting aquaporin-2 channels so water is reabsorbed regardless of plasma osmolality. The retained water dilutes plasma sodium. Mild volume expansion increases natriuretic signals and urinary sodium loss, so oedema does not develop and the patient appears euvolaemic. Sodium fell from 131 to 118 mmol/L over about two weeks. Because this developed over more than 48 hours it is classed as chronic: brain cells have partly adapted by losing osmolytes, but at this level water still enters neurons, causing cerebral oedema and his seizure. The same adaptation is why rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.

(c) A seizure means severe symptomatic hyponatraemia. He should be managed in a high-dependency setting with boluses of hypertonic saline given according to local protocol, aiming for a prompt rise of about 5 mmol/L, which usually relieves symptoms. Sodium is checked frequently. Total correction should be limited to around 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours, and lower in high-risk patients such as the malnourished or alcohol-dependent, to avoid osmotic demyelination. If the limit is exceeded, giving water or desmopressin can re-lower sodium.

Once stable, fluid restriction is the mainstay. Treating the underlying cancer with chemotherapy often improves SIADH. If restriction fails, specialist options include oral urea or a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist such as tolvaptan, which needs careful monitoring to avoid overcorrection. Hypotonic intravenous fluids should be avoided and other contributing drugs, such as SSRIs or opioids, reviewed.

questions.q: Mr Singh, 64, has CKD stage 4 and heart failure and recently started spironolactone alongside ramipril. He feels weak. K 7.1 mmol/L (non-haemolysed), creatinine 290 µmol/L (stable baseline 250). His pulse is 52 and regular. ECG shows tall peaked T waves and widened QRS. (a) Explain why he is hyperkalaemic. (b) Outline emergency management, explaining how each step works. (c) How would you prevent recurrence?
markScheme: Reduced GFR limits potassium excretion in CKD
ACE inhibitor lowers aldosterone; spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor, reducing ENaC-driven potassium secretion by principal cells
K 7.1 with ECG changes is a medical emergency needing cardiac monitoring
IV calcium to stabilise the myocardium (raises threshold potential); repeat if ECG changes persist; does not lower K
IV insulin with glucose shifts K into cells via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; monitor glucose for hypoglycaemia
Nebulised salbutamol as adjunct (beta-2 stimulation of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase)
Remove potassium: potassium binders (e.g. sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, patiromer) or dialysis if refractory
Stop spironolactone and review ramipril; repeat potassium regularly
Prevention: low-potassium diet advice, avoid NSAIDs and potassium supplements, regular monitoring after medication changes
Consider maintenance potassium binder to allow continuation of prognostically important RAAS inhibitors in heart failure
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Most potassium is excreted by principal cells of the collecting duct, which secrete potassium in exchange for sodium reabsorbed through ENaC under aldosterone control. Advanced CKD reduces the number of functioning nephrons and filtered load. Ramipril lowers angiotensin II and therefore aldosterone, and spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor, so potassium secretion is impaired at the same time as excretory capacity is reduced.

(b) Potassium above 6.5 mmol/L with ECG changes is an emergency. He needs continuous cardiac monitoring. IV calcium is given first; it restores the gap between resting membrane potential and threshold, protecting against arrhythmia within minutes, and is repeated if ECG changes persist. It does not lower potassium. IV insulin with glucose activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, moving potassium into cells within about 15 to 30 minutes; glucose prevents hypoglycaemia and capillary glucose is monitored for several hours. Nebulised salbutamol can be added as it also stimulates the pump. These shifts are temporary, so potassium must be removed. A potassium binder such as sodium zirconium cyclosilicate exchanges potassium in the gut. If potassium remains dangerously high or there is oliguric kidney failure, urgent dialysis is required. Spironolactone is stopped and ramipril withheld until potassium is safe, with repeated potassium measurements.

(c) Prevention includes dietetic advice on potassium intake, avoiding NSAIDs, potassium supplements and salt substitutes containing potassium, and checking potassium and renal function soon after starting or changing RAAS inhibitors. Because these drugs improve outcomes in heart failure, a maintenance potassium binder may allow them to be continued at a lower dose under specialist supervision. Metabolic acidosis in CKD should be corrected, as it also raises potassium.

questions.q: Mr Evans, 58, with a history of duodenal ulcers, has vomited large volumes after meals for a week. He is dehydrated. Na 138, K 2.9, Cl 88 mmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L. Gas: pH 7.50, pCO₂ 6.4 kPa (48 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 36 mmol/L. Urine chloride is under 10 mmol/L. (a) Interpret the gas. (b) Explain how the disorder is generated and maintained. (c) Outline management.
markScheme: Alkalaemia with raised bicarbonate: primary metabolic alkalosis
Raised pCO₂ represents appropriate respiratory compensation (hypoventilation)
Likely gastric outlet obstruction from peptic ulcer scarring causing vomiting
Generation: loss of gastric HCl; each H⁺ secreted generates a bicarbonate added to blood
Maintenance: volume depletion increases proximal sodium and bicarbonate reabsorption; aldosterone increases distal H⁺ and K⁺ secretion
Hypokalaemia from renal potassium loss (secondary hyperaldosteronism) and shifts; chloride depletion impairs bicarbonate excretion
Low urine chloride indicates saline-responsive (chloride-depleted) alkalosis
IV 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride replacement; monitor electrolytes
Nasogastric decompression; PPI; endoscopy to confirm cause and exclude malignancy
Definitive treatment: endoscopic balloon dilatation or surgery; H. pylori eradication if present
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The pH of 7.50 shows alkalaemia and the bicarbonate of 36 mmol/L identifies a metabolic alkalosis. The raised pCO₂ of 48 mmHg is respiratory compensation by hypoventilation. Using the common rule for metabolic alkalosis, expected pCO₂ is about 0.7 × 36 + 20 = 45 ± 5 mmHg, so compensation is appropriate. Post-prandial vomiting in a man with previous duodenal ulcers suggests gastric outlet obstruction from scarring.

(b) Parietal cells secrete H⁺ into the lumen and add an equivalent amount of bicarbonate to the blood. Normally this is balanced when acid reaches the duodenum and triggers pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. When gastric contents are vomited, the bicarbonate stays in the body, generating the alkalosis. It is maintained by the kidney. Volume depletion increases proximal reabsorption of sodium with bicarbonate, and chloride depletion limits the ability of intercalated cells to secrete bicarbonate in exchange for chloride. Secondary hyperaldosteronism increases distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions, causing hypokalaemia and sometimes paradoxical aciduria. The low urine chloride confirms a chloride-depleted, saline-responsive alkalosis.

(c) He needs IV 0.9% sodium chloride to restore volume and chloride, allowing the kidney to excrete excess bicarbonate, with potassium chloride added and electrolytes monitored. A nasogastric tube decompresses the stomach, and a PPI reduces acid secretion. Endoscopy confirms the cause and excludes gastric or duodenal cancer, with biopsies and H. pylori testing; infection is eradicated if present. Benign stenosis may respond to endoscopic balloon dilatation, while failure or malignancy needs surgery. Nutritional status should be assessed, as prolonged vomiting risks malnutrition and refeeding problems.

questions.q: Mr Hale, 40, is found confused with slurred speech; empty containers of antifreeze are nearby. Na 140, K 5.0, Cl 102, HCO₃⁻ 6 mmol/L, glucose 5 mmol/L, urea 6 mmol/L, creatinine 210 µmol/L, ionised calcium low. Measured osmolality 330 mOsm/kg. Gas: pH 7.15, pCO₂ 2.4 kPa (18 mmHg). Breath ethanol is zero. (a) Fully interpret the results with calculations. (b) Explain the toxicology. (c) Outline management and explain why time matters.
markScheme: Severe acidaemia; low bicarbonate: metabolic acidosis
Anion gap = 140 − (102 + 6) = 32 mmol/L: high anion gap
Winter's: predicted pCO₂ = 1.5 × 6 + 8 = 17 ± 2 mmHg; measured 18 mmHg, appropriate compensation
Calculated osmolality = 2 × 140 + 5 + 6 = 291 mOsm/kg; osmolar gap = 330 − 291 = 39 mOsm/kg (raised)
High anion gap plus high osmolar gap with no ethanol suggests toxic alcohol: ethylene glycol
Ethylene glycol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to glycolate and oxalate; glycolate causes acidosis
Oxalate combines with calcium forming calcium oxalate crystals: hypocalcaemia and AKI (crystals in urine)
Osmolar gap falls and anion gap rises as metabolism proceeds, so a normal osmolar gap later does not exclude poisoning
Seek specialist advice (TOXBASE/National Poisons Information Service); ABCDE
Block alcohol dehydrogenase with fomepizole (or ethanol if unavailable)
Haemodialysis removes parent compound and toxic metabolites and corrects acidosis and AKI
IV sodium bicarbonate for severe acidosis; treat symptomatic hypocalcaemia; cofactors thiamine and pyridoxine
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The pH of 7.15 and bicarbonate of 6 mmol/L show a severe metabolic acidosis. Anion gap = 140 − (102 + 6) = 32 mmol/L, which is markedly raised. Winter's formula predicts pCO₂ = 1.5 × 6 + 8 = 17 ± 2 mmHg, and the measured 18 mmHg shows appropriate respiratory compensation. Calculated osmolality = 2 × 140 + 5 + 6 = 291 mOsm/kg, so the osmolar gap is 330 − 291 = 39 mOsm/kg. A high anion gap with a high osmolar gap and no ethanol strongly suggests toxic alcohol poisoning; with antifreeze, AKI and hypocalcaemia, ethylene glycol is most likely. Lactate and ketones should still be measured.

(b) Ethylene glycol is itself relatively non-toxic but is osmotically active, causing the osmolar gap and inebriation. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts it to glycoaldehyde, then glycolic acid, the main cause of the acidosis, and ultimately oxalic acid. Oxalate binds calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals that deposit in renal tubules, causing AKI, and in other tissues, lowering ionised calcium. As metabolism proceeds, the osmolar gap falls while the anion gap rises, so a late presentation can show a normal osmolar gap.

(c) Management follows ABCDE with early advice from TOXBASE or the National Poisons Information Service and critical care involvement. The key antidote blocks alcohol dehydrogenase: fomepizole, or ethanol if it is unavailable, stopping production of toxic metabolites. Because he already has severe acidosis and AKI, haemodialysis is indicated; it removes both ethylene glycol and glycolate and corrects acidosis. IV sodium bicarbonate treats severe acidaemia and increases urinary elimination of acids. Symptomatic hypocalcaemia is corrected, though calcium is given cautiously because it may increase crystal formation. Thiamine and pyridoxine promote metabolism to less toxic products.

Time matters because toxicity comes from the metabolites. Early alcohol dehydrogenase blockade can prevent acidosis and renal injury, whereas late presentation needs dialysis and risks permanent kidney damage or death.

questions.q: Mr Walsh, 72, takes naproxen for osteoarthritis and aspirin for secondary prevention. He presents with two episodes of coffee-ground vomit and black tarry stools. Pulse 112, BP 94/58 mmHg, Hb 82 g/L (previously 135), urea 18 mmol/L. There are no signs of chronic liver disease. (a) What is the likely source and why? (b) Outline immediate management. (c) Outline management after endoscopy.
markScheme: Likely bleeding peptic (duodenal or gastric) ulcer caused by NSAID and aspirin
Melaena and disproportionately raised urea (digested blood protein and hypovolaemia) indicate upper GI source
Shock (tachycardia, hypotension) and high Glasgow-Blatchford score: high risk
ABCDE resuscitation, two large-bore cannulae, group and crossmatch, clotting
Transfuse red cells guided by haemodynamics and Hb; major haemorrhage protocol if needed
Stop NSAID and review aspirin; correct clotting abnormalities
Endoscopy immediately after resuscitation if unstable (within 24 hours for others)
Endoscopic haemostasis: combination of adrenaline injection with thermal or mechanical (clips) therapy
PPI after endoscopic haemostasis; test for H. pylori and eradicate if positive
If rebleeding: repeat endoscopy, interventional radiology embolisation or surgery; restart aspirin once haemostasis achieved, with PPI cover
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Coffee-ground vomiting and melaena indicate an upper GI bleed, and the urea of 18 mmol/L, raised out of proportion to creatinine, reflects absorbed blood protein and hypovolaemia. With naproxen and aspirin, both inhibiting COX-1 and gastroprotective prostaglandins, a bleeding peptic ulcer is most likely. Without signs of liver disease, varices are less likely but not excluded.

(b) He is shocked, with tachycardia, hypotension and a large haemoglobin fall, giving a high Glasgow-Blatchford score. Management follows ABCDE: oxygen if needed, two large-bore cannulae, bloods for full blood count, clotting, renal and liver function, and group and crossmatch. Crystalloid is given while blood is prepared, and red cells are transfused according to his haemodynamic state and haemoglobin; a major haemorrhage protocol is activated if bleeding is massive. Naproxen is stopped and aspirin withheld temporarily. Because he is unstable, endoscopy should take place immediately after resuscitation; stable patients have endoscopy within 24 hours. NICE advises against routinely starting PPIs before endoscopy in suspected non-variceal bleeding.

(c) At endoscopy, high-risk stigmata such as active bleeding or a visible vessel are treated with combination therapy: adrenaline injection plus a thermal or mechanical method such as clips, or other techniques. After endoscopic haemostasis a PPI is given to stabilise the clot. Biopsies or other testing for H. pylori are performed, with eradication if positive. Rebleeding is managed with repeat endoscopy, then interventional radiological embolisation or surgery. Aspirin for secondary prevention is usually restarted once haemostasis is secure, with ongoing PPI protection, and the NSAID is stopped permanently with alternative analgesia.

questions.q: Tom, 22, has had six months of crampy right iliac fossa pain, loose stools without blood and 6 kg weight loss. He smokes. Examination: tender right iliac fossa mass and a perianal fistula. Hb 108 g/L, MCV 102 fL, CRP 64 mg/L, albumin 31 g/L, faecal calprotectin markedly raised. (a) What is the likely diagnosis? Justify it. (b) How would you confirm it? (c) Outline management.
markScheme: Likely Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum with perianal disease
Features: RIF pain and mass, non-bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, perianal fistula, smoking, raised inflammatory markers
Macrocytosis suggests terminal ileal B12 malabsorption (folate deficiency also possible); check B12, folate, ferritin
Exclude infection (stool culture, C. difficile); consider differential (intestinal TB, lymphoma, appendix mass)
Ileocolonoscopy with biopsies: patchy transmural inflammation, granulomas
Cross-sectional imaging: MR enterography (small bowel extent, strictures) and pelvic MRI for perianal disease
Smoking cessation is the most effective modifiable intervention
Induction: corticosteroids (budesonide for mild ileocaecal disease) or early biologic for high-risk disease; exclusive enteral nutrition is an option
Maintenance: thiopurine or methotrexate, or biologic therapy (anti-TNF, vedolizumab, ustekinumab-type); anti-TNF used for perianal fistulae with surgical drainage/seton
Surgery for strictures, abscess or refractory disease (ileocaecal resection); nutritional support, B12 replacement and bone protection
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The most likely diagnosis is Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum with perianal involvement. Supporting features are a young smoker with chronic right iliac fossa pain and mass, non-bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, a perianal fistula, raised CRP, low albumin and a high faecal calprotectin. The macrocytic anaemia suggests B12 malabsorption from terminal ileal disease, although folate deficiency, medication or mixed deficiency must be checked; iron deficiency may coexist.

(b) Stool cultures and C. difficile testing exclude infection. Ileocolonoscopy with biopsies is the key test and may show patchy ulceration with deep fissures and, histologically, transmural inflammation and non-caseating granulomas. MR enterography defines the extent of small bowel disease, strictures and fistulae, and a pelvic MRI maps the perianal fistula and any abscess. Intestinal tuberculosis, lymphoma and an appendix mass are considered in the differential.

(c) Stopping smoking is essential because smoking increases relapse and need for surgery. Nutritional status is assessed and B12, iron and folate deficiencies corrected. Remission can be induced with a corticosteroid, for example budesonide for mild ileocaecal disease or systemic steroids for more active disease, and exclusive enteral nutrition is an alternative. Steroids are not used for maintenance. Given his young age, perianal disease and extensive inflammation, he has poor prognostic features, so early biologic therapy such as an anti-TNF agent, often combined with a thiopurine, is appropriate. Anti-TNF therapy is effective for perianal fistulae alongside surgical drainage of sepsis and seton placement. Other options include vedolizumab, ustekinumab or JAK inhibitors. Surgery, such as ileocaecal resection, is needed for fibrotic strictures, abscesses or refractory disease. Bone health and vaccination before immunosuppression should not be forgotten.

questions.q: Sophie, 29, has fatigue, bloating and loose stools. Hb 96 g/L, MCV 72 fL, ferritin 6 µg/L. She has type 1 diabetes, a sister with hypothyroidism, and an itchy blistering rash on her elbows and buttocks. She eats a normal diet including bread and pasta. (a) What is the most likely diagnosis? (b) How should it be confirmed? (c) Outline management and long-term complications.
markScheme: Likely coeliac disease: iron deficiency anaemia, GI symptoms, type 1 diabetes association
Rash suggests dermatitis herpetiformis, the skin manifestation of coeliac disease
Serology: IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA, while eating gluten (IgG-based tests if IgA deficient)
Confirm with duodenal biopsies at endoscopy: villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, raised intraepithelial lymphocytes
Must continue gluten before testing to avoid false negatives
Lifelong strict gluten-free diet with dietitian support
Iron replacement; check folate, B12, calcium, vitamin D
Assess bone health (DXA where indicated) because of osteoporosis risk
Complications: osteoporosis, refractory coeliac disease, enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma and small bowel adenocarcinoma, hyposplenism (vaccination)
Annual review with serology to check adherence; offer serological testing to first-degree relatives (NICE NG20)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The most likely diagnosis is coeliac disease. She has iron deficiency anaemia with very low ferritin, bloating and loose stools, and type 1 diabetes, which shares HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 susceptibility.
