The itchy blistering rash on extensor surfaces suggests dermatitis herpetiformis, the cutaneous form of the disease.

(b) The first test is IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA, because IgA deficiency is more common in coeliac disease and gives false negatives; IgG-based tests are used if she is IgA deficient. She must be eating gluten for at least six weeks before testing. Duodenal biopsies at upper GI endoscopy confirm the diagnosis, showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and raised intraepithelial lymphocytes. Current guidance allows some adults with very high antibody levels to be diagnosed without biopsy after specialist review. Skin biopsy can confirm dermatitis herpetiformis.

(c) Treatment is a lifelong strict gluten-free diet, supported by a specialist dietitian and coeliac support organisations. Iron is replaced, and folate, B12, calcium and vitamin D are checked and corrected. The rash responds to the diet, though dapsone may be needed initially for symptom control. Bone density assessment is considered because malabsorption increases osteoporosis risk. Because coeliac disease can cause functional hyposplenism, pneumococcal and other vaccinations are reviewed. She should have annual review including weight, symptoms, dietary adherence and serology. Persistent symptoms despite a strict diet raise concern about inadvertent gluten exposure, refractory coeliac disease or complications such as enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma or small bowel adenocarcinoma, whose risks fall with good adherence. Her diabetes team should know, as malabsorption may affect glucose control, and her first-degree relatives should be offered serological testing.

questions.q: Mr Price, 55, has alcohol-related cirrhosis and still drinks. He presents with increasing abdominal swelling, fever, mild abdominal tenderness and confusion. He has flapping tremor and shifting dullness. Bilirubin 68 µmol/L, albumin 26 g/L, INR 1.8, Na 128 mmol/L, creatinine 140 µmol/L. Ascitic tap: neutrophils 420 cells/mm³, ascitic albumin 9 g/L, serum albumin 26 g/L. (a) Interpret the ascitic results. (b) Explain the pathophysiology of his ascites and confusion. (c) Outline management.
markScheme: SAAG = 26 − 9 = 17 g/L (11 or more): portal hypertensive ascites
Ascitic neutrophils above 250 cells/mm³: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Decompensated cirrhosis with SBP precipitating hepatic encephalopathy and probable AKI
Ascites: portal hypertension plus splanchnic vasodilatation (nitric oxide) reduces effective arterial volume, activating RAAS, sympathetic system and ADH, causing sodium and water retention
Hypoalbuminaemia lowers oncotic pressure; hyponatraemia from ADH-driven water retention
Encephalopathy: ammonia and other gut-derived toxins bypass the liver through portosystemic shunts and failing hepatocytes; triggered by infection
Empirical IV antibiotics (e.g. third-generation cephalosporin class per local policy) and send ascitic culture in blood culture bottles
IV human albumin solution in SBP to reduce risk of hepatorenal syndrome; stop diuretics and nephrotoxins while AKI present
Lactulose (aim 2–3 soft stools/day) and rifaximin for encephalopathy; avoid sedatives; search for other precipitants (GI bleed, constipation, electrolytes)

Long-term: alcohol cessation with support, nutrition and thiamine, secondary SBP prophylaxis, sodium restriction and diuretics once renal function recovers, variceal screening and HCC surveillance, transplant assessment if abstinent
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The serum-ascites albumin gradient is 26 − 9 = 17 g/L. A gradient of 11 g/L or more indicates portal hypertensive ascites, consistent with cirrhosis. An ascitic neutrophil count of 420 cells/mm³ exceeds 250, diagnosing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

(b) Cirrhosis raises resistance to portal flow, causing portal hypertension. Splanchnic vasodilatation, mainly through nitric oxide, reduces effective arterial blood volume. The body responds by activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system and ADH, so the kidneys retain sodium and water. Combined with high sinusoidal pressure and low albumin, fluid leaks into the peritoneum. ADH-driven water retention explains his hyponatraemia, and intense renal vasoconstriction can progress to hepatorenal syndrome. His confusion and flapping tremor indicate hepatic encephalopathy: ammonia and other gut-derived neurotoxins escape hepatic clearance through portosystemic shunts and failing hepatocytes, causing astrocyte swelling. Infection, here SBP, is a common trigger.

(c) He needs empirical intravenous antibiotics according to local policy, with ascitic fluid sent in blood culture bottles and blood cultures taken. Intravenous human albumin solution is given in SBP because it reduces the risk of renal failure and death. Diuretics and nephrotoxic drugs are stopped while creatinine is raised. Encephalopathy is treated with lactulose titrated to two or three soft stools a day, with rifaximin to prevent recurrence, while sedatives are avoided and other precipitants such as GI bleeding, constipation, hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance are sought. Parenteral thiamine is given and alcohol withdrawal managed.

Longer term he needs support for alcohol abstinence, the most important determinant of prognosis, plus nutritional input, secondary SBP prophylaxis, sodium restriction with spironolactone once renal function recovers, endoscopic variceal screening and six-monthly HCC ultrasound surveillance. Referral for transplant assessment can be considered if he stops drinking.

questions.q: 'Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is better understood as a disease of the metabolic system than of the liver.' Discuss this statement, covering terminology, pathogenesis, risk stratification and management.
markScheme: 2023 multisociety consensus renamed NAFLD as MASLD: steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor; MASH replaces NASH; MetALD for those with higher alcohol intake
Strong associations with obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension (metabolic syndrome)
Pathogenesis: insulin resistance increases adipose lipolysis and hepatic de novo lipogenesis; lipotoxicity, oxidative stress, inflammation and stellate cell activation drive fibrosis
Genetic modifiers (e.g. PNPLA3, TM6SF2) and gut microbiome show liver-specific susceptibility
Most patients die of cardiovascular disease and extrahepatic cancer rather than liver disease
Fibrosis stage is the main predictor of liver-related outcomes; progression to cirrhosis and HCC
Risk stratification: FIB-4 then ELF test or transient elastography; refer if advanced fibrosis
Management: weight loss (around 7–10% improves steatohepatitis and fibrosis), diet and exercise, alcohol reduction
Treat cardiometabolic risk: statins safe and indicated, diabetes drugs with liver benefit (GLP-1 receptor agonists, pioglitazone)
Bariatric surgery can reverse disease; liver-targeted therapy emerging (resmetirom FDA accelerated approval 2024); cirrhosis needs HCC and variceal surveillance
Balanced conclusion: metabolic origin but liver-specific consequences require hepatic assessment
questions.modelAnswer:
In 2023 an international consensus replaced 'non-alcoholic fatty liver disease' with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), defined by hepatic steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor, such as raised BMI or waist circumference, dysglycaemia, hypertension or dyslipidaemia. NASH became MASH, and MetALD describes overlap with higher alcohol intake. The change itself supports the statement: the disease is now defined by metabolic dysfunction rather than the absence of alcohol.

Pathogenesis is rooted in insulin resistance. Resistant adipose tissue releases excess fatty acids, while hyperinsulinaemia drives hepatic de novo lipogenesis. When fat delivery exceeds the liver's capacity to oxidise or export it, lipotoxic species cause hepatocyte stress, inflammation and stellate cell activation, leading to fibrosis. MASLD is closely associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes, and the leading causes of death are cardiovascular disease and extrahepatic cancers rather than liver failure.

However, liver-specific factors matter. Genetic variants such as PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 increase susceptibility to inflammation and fibrosis, and only a minority progress to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. Fibrosis stage is the strongest predictor of liver-related outcomes, so risk stratification is hepatic: a FIB-4 score, followed by the ELF blood test or transient elastography for indeterminate or high results, and referral for advanced fibrosis. Cirrhosis requires HCC surveillance and variceal assessment.

Management combines both views. Sustained weight loss of around 7 to 10% improves steatohepatitis and can regress fibrosis, through diet, exercise, GLP-1 based therapies or bariatric surgery. Cardiovascular risk is aggressively treated, and statins are safe and indicated. Pioglitazone and GLP-1 receptor agonists have shown histological benefit, and resmetirom, a liver-targeted thyroid hormone receptor beta agonist, received US accelerated approval in 2024.

The statement is largely correct about cause and the main cause of death, but a purely metabolic view would miss the liver-specific assessment that identifies those at risk of cirrhosis. MASLD is best seen as a metabolic disease with a hepatic phenotype requiring targeted hepatology input.

questions.q: Chloe, 19, with anorexia nervosa, is admitted with BMI 13.5 kg/m² after eating almost nothing for two weeks. Baseline phosphate 0.85 mmol/L, potassium 3.3 mmol/L, magnesium 0.68 mmol/L. Nasogastric feeding is started. On day 3 she is breathless with ankle oedema; phosphate is 0.35 mmol/L. (a) What has happened? (b) Explain the pathophysiology. (c) How should this be managed, and how could it have been reduced?
markScheme: Refeeding syndrome with severe hypophosphataemia and fluid overload
High-risk features: BMI below 16, minimal intake for over 10 days or near-starvation, low baseline electrolytes
Starvation: adaptation to fat and ketone metabolism with depletion of intracellular phosphate, potassium, magnesium and thiamine despite near-normal serum values
Feeding carbohydrate triggers insulin release, driving phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and increasing thiamine use
Phosphate depletion lowers ATP and 2,3-DPG: respiratory muscle weakness, cardiac failure, arrhythmias, seizures, haemolysis
Insulin causes renal sodium and water retention leading to oedema and heart failure
Management: slow or pause feeding, IV phosphate, potassium and magnesium replacement, cardiac monitoring, careful fluid balance
Thiamine and B vitamin supplementation
Prevention: start at low energy intake and increase gradually over days, pre-feeding electrolyte correction or concurrent supplementation, daily bloods initially
Multidisciplinary care including eating disorder psychiatry; follow MEED guidance (RCPsych 2022) on medical risk
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Chloe has refeeding syndrome, with severe hypophosphataemia and fluid retention causing breathlessness and oedema, probably early cardiac failure.

(b) In starvation the body shifts from carbohydrate to fat and ketone metabolism, insulin falls and intracellular stores of phosphate, potassium and magnesium become depleted, even though serum levels may look near normal. Thiamine stores also fall. When feeding begins, carbohydrate triggers insulin secretion. Insulin drives glucose, phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells for glycogen synthesis and ATP production, so serum levels fall abruptly, and the demand for thiamine as a cofactor rises. Severe hypophosphataemia reduces ATP and red cell 2,3-DPG, causing respiratory muscle weakness, impaired myocardial contractility, arrhythmias, seizures, rhabdomyolysis and haemolysis. Insulin also causes renal sodium and water retention, and in a heart already weakened by starvation this leads to oedema and heart failure. Thiamine deficiency can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.

(c) Feeding should be slowed or paused with dietetic and medical review. Phosphate is replaced intravenously given the severity, with potassium and magnesium corrected, as hypomagnesaemia impairs potassium and phosphate correction. She needs cardiac monitoring, careful fluid balance, daily weight and consideration of diuretics for overload. Thiamine and other B vitamins are given. Electrolytes are checked at least daily until stable, and feeding is reintroduced gradually.

Prevention starts with recognising high risk: BMI below 16, very low intake for more than 10 days and low baseline electrolytes all apply. NICE recommends starting nutrition at a low energy level and increasing slowly over several days, with thiamine before and during feeding, oral or IV electrolyte supplementation and daily monitoring. The RCPsych MEED guidance (2022) also stresses multidisciplinary care, avoiding both underfeeding and refeeding complications, with eating disorder psychiatry, dietitians and physicians working together.

questions.q: 'GLP-1-based drugs will make bariatric surgery obsolete.' Evaluate this proposition with reference to physiology, trial evidence, safety, access and cost.
markScheme: Physiology: GLP-1 receptor agonists (and dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists) act on hypothalamic and brainstem satiety pathways, slow gastric emptying and enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion
Bariatric surgery also alters gut hormones (raised GLP-1 and PYY after bypass), not only restriction
STEP 1 (2021): semaglutide gave mean weight loss around 15% versus about 2% with placebo
SURMOUNT-1 (2022): tirzepatide gave mean weight loss around 20% at the highest dose
SELECT (2023): semaglutide reduced major adverse cardiovascular events by about 20% in people with obesity and cardiovascular disease without diabetes
Weight regain after stopping drugs (STEP 1 extension); treatment probably needs to be long term
Surgery produces typically greater and durable weight loss (around 25–30%), high diabetes remission (STAMPEDE) and reduced mortality (Swedish Obese Subjects study)

Drug safety: gastrointestinal effects, gallbladder disease, pancreatitis concerns, lean mass loss; surgical risks: perioperative complications, micronutrient deficiencies, dumping, need for lifelong follow-up
Access: NICE restrictions (semaglutide within specialist weight management, time-limited; tirzepatide phased rollout), supply constraints, cost of indefinite therapy
Complementary roles: drugs before surgery, after surgery for regain, or for people unsuitable for or declining surgery
Reasoned conclusion: likely to reduce but not eliminate demand for surgery
questions.modelAnswer:
GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide, and the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide, act on hypothalamic and brainstem pathways to increase satiety, slow gastric emptying and enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion. Bariatric surgery works partly through the same physiology: after Roux-en-Y bypass and sleeve gastrectomy, post-meal GLP-1 and PYY rise and ghrelin may fall. The two treatments therefore overlap more than a simple 'pill versus restriction' contrast implies.

Trial evidence for the drugs is impressive. In STEP 1 (2021), semaglutide produced mean weight loss of about 15% against about 2% with placebo, and in SURMOUNT-1 (2022), tirzepatide achieved about 20% at the highest dose. SELECT (2023) showed that semaglutide reduced major cardiovascular events by about 20% in people with obesity and established cardiovascular disease without diabetes. These results approach surgical outcomes without operative risk.

However, surgery still produces greater and more durable weight loss, often 25 to 30% of body weight, and long-term data are much stronger. The Swedish Obese Subjects study showed reduced mortality over many years, and STAMPEDE showed higher diabetes remission with surgery than intensive medical therapy. When the drugs are stopped, much of the lost weight returns, as the STEP 1 extension showed, so they probably need to be continued indefinitely. Long-term safety is less certain: gastrointestinal effects are common and gallbladder disease and loss of lean mass occur. Surgery has its own risks, including complications, micronutrient deficiency and dumping, and requires lifelong follow-up.

Access matters. At the time of writing, NICE had approved semaglutide only within specialist weight management services for a limited period, and tirzepatide through a phased rollout, reflecting the cost of treating a large population indefinitely and recent supply shortages. Surgery is a single, more expensive intervention but may be more cost-effective over decades.

The proposition is overstated. GLP-1-based drugs will reduce demand for surgery and extend effective treatment to many more people, but surgery is likely to remain important for severe obesity, for people who cannot tolerate or afford long-term drug therapy, and in combination with drugs before or after surgery.
